questions.question: Visual input from the eyes is primarily processed in which lobe of the cerebral cortex?
questions.explanation: Visual input travels to the primary visual sensory area located in the occipital lobe, at the back of the cerebrum, where it is initially processed before being passed to visual association areas.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Forebrain: Cerebrum, Sensory and Motor Functions

questions.question: Sensations of touch, pain, and pressure (somatosensory input) arrive at the region of the cortex located:

options.B: In the parietal lobe, on the gyrus immediately behind the central sulcus
options.C: In the temporal lobe, buried in the lateral fissure
options.D: Only in the cerebellum, never the cerebrum

questions.explanation: Somatosensory signals (touch, pain, pressure) reach the primary somatosensory cortex, located in the parietal lobe on the gyrus immediately behind the central sulcus — right next to the primary motor cortex, which lies on the gyrus just in front of the central sulcus.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Sensory and Motor Functions

questions.question: Damage to the motor cortex on the LEFT side of the brain will typically produce movement weakness on which side of the body?

options.B: The right side (opposite side), because motor fibers cross to the other side below the head
options.D: Neither side — motor cortex damage never affects limb movement

questions.explanation: Fibers from the motor cortex on one side of the brain cross to the opposite side of the body on their way down to the spinal cord. So damage to the left motor cortex produces weakness, loss of dexterity, or spastic paralysis on the right side of the body below the head.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Sensory and Motor Functions

questions.question: Which two limbic system structures are most strongly implicated in the formation of new memories?

options.A: The olfactory bulb and septal nuclei
options.C: The cingulate gyrus and corpus callosum

questions.explanation: Among the limbic system structures (olfactory bulb, septal nuclei, hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus), the hippocampus and amygdala in particular play a key role in the formation of new memories — as dramatically illustrated by the case of patient H.M., whose bilateral removal of these structures left him unable to form new long-term memories.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Forebrain: Limbic System

questions.question: A hallmark intellectual deficit seen after prefrontal-lobe damage, distinct from a general drop in IQ (which is often unaffected), is:

options.A: Complete loss of the ability to speak
options.B: Difficulty planning and sequencing actions, plus perseveration (continuing a behaviour even when the situation demands a new response)
options.D: Immediate loss of all long-term memories formed before the injury

questions.explanation: While standard IQ tests are often little affected by prefrontal damage, patients show subtle but characteristic deficits: difficulty planning a sequence of actions, and perseveration — a tendency to keep behaving the same way even when circumstances call for a different response.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Frontal-Lobe Association Cortex

questions.question: A patient with damage to the RIGHT parietal association cortex draws a clock face but only completes the right half, leaving the left side blank, and is unaware anything is missing. This phenomenon is known as:
questions.explanation: Contralateral neglect is a classic sign of right parietal association cortex damage: patients ignore the left side of space and their own body (the side opposite/contralateral to the damaged hemisphere), often while denying anything is wrong.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Parietal-Lobe Association Cortex

questions.question: A patient can clearly feel that they are touching an object (their sense of touch is intact) but cannot identify what the object is by touch alone. This deficit in recognition is called:
questions.explanation: Agnosia is a deficit in recognition despite intact basic sensation — the patient knows they are touching something but cannot identify what it is. When this occurs specifically with touch, it is called tactile agnosia, commonly seen after parietal-lobe damage.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Parietal-Lobe Association Cortex

questions.question: Damage to Wernicke's area, located in the left temporal lobe, characteristically produces speech that is:

options.A: Completely absent — the patient cannot make any sound
options.B: Fluent in output but conveying little actual meaning, with impaired understanding of speech and written language
options.C: Slow and effortful but perfectly meaningful
options.D: Normal in every respect except pitch

questions.explanation: Wernicke's area damage markedly impairs comprehension of spoken and written language. Characteristically, the patient's own speech remains fluent in its flow and rhythm but conveys little coherent meaning.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Temporal-Lobe Association Cortex, Language Functions

questions.question: Following bilateral removal of the hippocampus and amygdala (to control severe epilepsy), the famous patient H.M. could still learn new motor/perceptual skills (like tracing a mirror-image star) without any conscious memory of having practiced them before. This dissociation illustrates the difference between:

options.B: Procedural memory (how to do things) and declarative memory (memory of specific events)
options.D: Retrograde amnesia and anterograde amnesia only, with no other distinction

questions.explanation: H.M. retained procedural memory — he could learn and improve at tasks like mirror-tracing or the Tower of Hanoi over repeated sessions — even though he had no declarative (event) memory of ever having done the task before. This case was pivotal in showing procedural and declarative memory are at least partly separate systems.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Temporal-Lobe Association Cortex, Memory Functions

questions.question: Despite his severe memory problems, patient H.M. had relatively normal short-term memory (e.g. could repeat six numbers forward after hearing them once) and intact memories from before his operation. What was specifically impaired?

options.A: His ability to form new long-term memories
options.B: His personality and IQ, both of which dropped sharply
options.C: His sense of touch and vision
options.D: His ability to speak or understand language

questions.explanation: H.M.'s deficit was specifically in forming new long-term memories (anterograde amnesia) — his immediate/short-term memory and his remote memories from before the surgery were largely preserved, illustrating that short-term and long-term memory, and the process of consolidating one into the other, are at least partly separable.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Temporal-Lobe Association Cortex, Memory Functions

questions.question: In most right-handed people, which cerebral hemisphere is specialized for language functions?

options.C: Both hemispheres equally, with no lateralization
options.D: Neither — language is controlled entirely by the cerebellum

questions.explanation: In roughly 95% of right-handed people (and about 65% of left-handed people), the left hemisphere is specialized for language functions, as shown by sodium-amytal testing and by the much higher rate of language problems following left-hemisphere strokes.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Left- and Right-Hemisphere Functions

questions.question: The hypothalamus regulates the body's internal environment (temperature, blood salt concentration, hormone levels) chiefly by controlling secretions from which gland?

options.C: The adrenal gland directly, bypassing the pituitary entirely

questions.explanation: The hypothalamus is connected to the pituitary gland and controls its hormone secretion into the bloodstream, either through nerve impulses or chemical releasing factors — linking the nervous system to the body's broader glandular (endocrine) system.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Forebrain: Hypothalamus and Pituitary

questions.question: The corpus callosum's main function is to:

options.A: Produce hormones for the endocrine system
options.B: Connect corresponding areas of the cortex in one cerebral hemisphere with the other hemisphere
options.C: Carry sound information from the ear to the temporal lobe

questions.explanation: The corpus callosum is a large bundle of nerve fibers that connects corresponding areas of the cortex in the left and right cerebral hemispheres, allowing communication and integration between the two sides of the brain.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Forebrain: Cerebrum, Structure

questions.question: Association areas of the cerebral cortex (in the frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes) are now understood to primarily:

options.A: Simply form a direct wired connection between sensory input and motor output with no further processing
options.B: Process and integrate sensory information relayed from primary sensory areas and the thalamus, supporting complex functions like thought, memory, and language
options.C: Have no known function at all
options.D: Exist only in non-human animals, not in humans

questions.explanation: Early researchers thought association areas simply linked sensory input to motor output directly, but they are now understood to process and integrate information from primary sensory areas and the thalamus, supporting higher psychological functions such as thought, memory, imagery, and language before that processed information may be passed on to motor areas.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Association Cortex, Behavior, and Experience
